content_voiceover: This question asks which statement about prognostic factors in adult ALL is wrong, and the answer is A. It's incorrect to say that failing to achieve complete remission within four weeks is regarded as unfavorable in most adult ALL studies, in reality, that four-week induction failure threshold is not the standard cutoff most studies use, early response is instead typically judged by blast clearance at day seven, day fourteen, or day twenty-one, which is exactly what statements B and C describe correctly. Persistent blasts between days seven and twenty-one of induction, and early peripheral blast persistence at day seven specifically, are both genuine markers of chemotherapy resistance and unfavorable prognosis. Statement D is accurate, RQ-PCR-based BCR-ABL1 measurable residual disease monitoring in Philadelphia-positive ALL is prognostic at multiple timepoints, during therapy, after completing therapy, and after transplant, and the MD Anderson data cited, seventy-one percent relapse-free survival with TKI plus intensive chemo in those achieving complete molecular response by three months, is correctly reported. Statement E is also accurate, describing the E1910 trial, where adding blinatumomab to consolidation chemotherapy significantly improved overall survival in MRD-negative BCP-ALL.
keypoints: 4-week CR failure is NOT the standard early-response cutoff in adult ALL
Real early-response markers: blast clearance at day 7, 14, or 21
BCR-ABL1 MRD by RQ-PCR is prognostic during/after therapy and post-HSCT
E1910 trial: adding blinatumomab to consolidation improved OS in MRD-negative BCP-ALL
keypoint_voiceover: For adult ALL prognosis, the day counts matter more than a four-week cutoff, early blast clearance at day seven, fourteen, or twenty-one is what predicts outcome. And remember the E1910 trial result, adding blinatumomab to consolidation improved overall survival specifically in MRD-negative B-cell precursor ALL, a landmark finding for the boards.
